newsitem.title: USA: Republican Congress off to slow, slow start.
newsitem.headline: Republican Congress off to slow, slow start.

text.p: The idleness of March is upon Congress, the House floor largely empty of lawmakers and the Senate stymied as Republicans once again failed to pass a balanced budget constitutional amendment.

A lackadaisical schedule and high profile defeats on the few substantive issues considered so far, such as the budget amendment, term limits and family planning aid, has bred worry among Republicans and promises of a more aggressive pace.
On Thursday House leaders will unveil a list of 12 legislative priorities, including a balanced budget, tax cuts, environmental issues and a ban on certain late-term abortions.
Lawmakers call the plan a start, but only that.

"The big picture in my mind is budget negotiations" with the White House, said Florida Republican Rep. Joe Scarborough. "The president has dominated the agenda since (last year's government) shutdown. It's time we moved beyond this sort of shellshocked state we've been in."
Two years ago the Capitol was crammed with red-eyed, sleep-starved legislators fighting the calendar to pass the newly powerful Republicans' 100-day Contract with America.
Now members of Congress look rested, if a bit bored, on those occasions when the House is in session. The Senate has logged more hours, but not gotten much better results.

Speaker Newt Gingrich has sunk largely out of public view, after a House vote in January to reprimand him for ethics violations. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott has taken the lead but failed on the budget amendment, his top priority.

Republican leaders protest the slower pace is merely a return to business as usual, calling the Contract with America a historic exception to the usual drill. They say the quiet is deceptive, with action aplenty off the House floor.

"This Congress is one where the normal committee process is working .... (It) looks like the proverbial duck floating on the pond, underneath he paddles like hell," said California Republican Rep. Christopher Cox.
Congress has sent President Clinton four bills, including an airline ticket tax and release of international family planning funds -- hardly top Republican priorities.
A constitutional amendment setting term limits for lawmakers, a priority of House leaders, got nowhere near the two-thirds majority needed.

Wednesday the House voted to congratulate Guatemala and Nicaragua for moves toward democracy, commend retired Secretary of State Warren Christopher and support display of the Ten Commandments in public buildings.

"We are indeed legislating. We are in a congratulatory legislative mode. This week we will be congratulating Guatemala, Nicaragua, Warren Christopher and Moses," said Massachusetts Democratic Rep. Barney Frank.
Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt complained the House is "sliding into irrelevance."
In the Senate the biggest substantive vote has been a constitutional amendment to balance the budget, which failed by one vote for the second session in a row.

Lott, who unveiled an 11-part legislative plan, has also become bogged down in an unexpected battle over funding for an investigation into Democratic campaign irregularities. Senate Republicans picked up seats in the elections, but do not have 60 votes to prevent a Democratic filibuster.
How slow is the pace? By Feb. 28, 1995, the House had been in session 296 hours, the Senate 316. By the same date this year, the House had met 58 hours, the Senate 134.
Compared to other years following a presidential election, the pace is slow. By the end of February 1993 the House had met 111 hours, the Senate 116.
In a memo, House Majority Leader Dick Armey promised action on the budget, taxes, family leave, NATO expansion, transportation, education, the environment and more.
"When this Congress is over we will have a record we can be proud of," said Florida Republican Rep. Charles Canady. "I do think things have been slow. I think they'll pick up."
